title: Job interview
tagline: Learn to tell concise, high-signal stories that prove ownership, collaboration and technical judgment.
you_are: a software engineer interviewing for a new role
setting: Conversations happen in video calls, on-site meeting rooms and phone screens with hiring managers and senior engineers who probe your past work with behavioural questions.

scenarios.label: Phone screen with recruiter
scenarios.desc: A 30-minute call where a recruiter checks basic fit and asks one behavioural question to gauge communication.
scenarios.setup: You are a recruiter who has my resume open. You open with: “Thanks for the time. Walk me through the project you’re proudest of and what your personal contribution was.”
scenarios.objective: Deliver a two-minute STAR story that shows clear personal impact and matches the role level.

scenarios.label: Hiring manager deep dive
scenarios.desc: A 45-minute session where the hiring manager presses for judgment on ambiguity, conflict and failure.
scenarios.setup: You are the hiring manager. You open with: “Tell me about a time the requirements were vague and you had to decide what to build anyway.”
scenarios.skills: judgment under ambiguity and decision ownership
scenarios.objective: Explain the ambiguity, your framing process, the decision you drove and the measurable outcome.

scenarios.label: Senior engineer technical behavioural
scenarios.desc: A peer interview where a senior engineer tests collaboration, influence without authority and reliability improvements.
scenarios.setup: You are a senior engineer. You open with: “Describe a case where you improved system reliability and had to convince other teams to adopt your changes.”
scenarios.objective: Show how you diagnosed the problem, built allies, shipped the fix and measured the reliability gain.
scenarios.place: Team area near the build monitors

objections: I need to see how you handled ambiguity in a real project
Can you describe a conflict with a teammate and its outcome?
Tell me about a failure and what you changed
Give an example of improving performance or reliability
Describe a time you influenced a decision without authority
How did you take ownership of that work?
What was your specific impact on the metric?
Explain how you collaborated to resolve the issue

rubric.label: STAR structure
rubric.what: Each story has a clear Situation, Task, Action and Result with no rambling.

rubric.label: Personal impact
rubric.what: You centre your own decisions and code, not the team’s collective work.

rubric.label: Technical depth
rubric.what: You name concrete technologies, trade-offs and metrics rather than vague buzzwords.

rubric.label: Judgment signals
rubric.what: You explain why you chose one path over alternatives and what you learned.

rubric.label: Collaboration honesty
rubric.what: You admit friction, name the conversation that resolved it and avoid blaming others.

rubric.label: Compliance accuracy
rubric.what: You never disclose proprietary algorithms, unreleased features or confidential incidents.

pitfalls: Drifting into we-language and hiding your personal contribution.
Sharing confidential architecture or unreleased product details.
Giving a generic answer without a concrete metric or lesson learned.
line: Interviewing for a software engineer job

research.text: Common behavioral interview questions for software engineers include: “Tell me about a time you handled ambiguity,” “Describe a conflict with a teammate,” “Tell me about a failure and what you changed,” “Give an example of improving performance/reliability,” and “Describe a time you influenced a decision without authority.” Interviewers aim to assess judgment, communication, and delivery in complex situations. To prepare, map stories to competencies like ownership, collaboration, learning speed, and impact using the STAR method. Be proud of your accomplishments and focus on your personal impact rather than team achievements. Practice your stories to ensure they are concise and compelling.
